title-group.article-title: LES of transient flows controlled by DBD plasma actuator over a stalled airfoil
title-group.alt-title: International Journal of Computational Fluid Dynamics

contrib-group.aff: bInstitute of Space and Astronautics Science, JAXA, Sagamihara,Japan

abstract.p: Large-eddy simulations (LES) are employed to understand the flow field over a NACA 0015 airfoil controlled by a dielectric barrier discharge (DBD) plasma actuator. The Suzen body force model is utilised to introduce the effect of the DBD plasma actuator. The Reynolds number is fixed at 63,000. Transient processes arising due to non-dimensional excitation frequencies of one and six are discussed. The time required to establish flow authority is between four and six characteristic times, independent of the excitation frequency. If the separation is suppressed, the initial flow conditions do not affect the quasi-steady state, and the lift coefficient of the higher frequency case converges very quickly. The transient states can be categorised into following three stages: (1) the lift and drag decreasing stage, (2) the lift recovery stage, and (3) the lift and drag converging stage. The development of vortices and their influence on control is delineated. The simulations show that in the initial transient state, separation of flow suppression is closely related to the development spanwise vortices while during the later, quasi-steady state, three-dimensional vortices become more important.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Separation occurs in various fluidic devices, such as for example, wing sections and turbine blades. In most cases, the effect of separation is detrimental to the performance of the device. For example, when the flow separation occurs on the wing of an aircraft in flight, the lift decreases while the drag increases, which leads to a worsening of fuel consumption and can sometimes threaten the stability of the aircraft. Separation control has thus seen continuous investigation over the past several decades.

Passive devices, such as vortex generators, are widely utilised, but only perform well at design (cruise) conditions and cannot flexibly respond to various changes in the flight envelope. On the other hand, active flow control can be adapted to be effective at a wide range of conditions, but require additional mechanisms and effort to determine the parameters. While conventional active flow-control devices need complex mechanical systems, active flow control with micro-scale devices are getting increasing attention in recent decades, especially in low-Reynolds-number flow regions because of the increasing demand of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) and micro-air vehicles (MAVs) in the industrial and disaster-relief fields. A micro-device can dynamically control a global flow field by inputting a low momentum in a small local region (Mueller and DeLaurier 2003). This is in contrast to conventional steady jets, which often require significant momentum to be imparted into the boundary layer for separation control. Dielectric barrier discharge (DBD) plasma actuators (Post and Corke 2004; Corke, Lon Enloe, and Wilkinson 2010) (hereafter, plasma actuator) and synthetic jets (Seifert, Theofilis, and Joslin 2002; Okada et al. 2010) have been widely studied by many researchers because of their relatively low energy consumption, a high responsiveness, and a broad range of frequencies. The plasma actuator is more recent of the two, and is being increasingly employed because of its simpler structure and versatility. For example, a flush-mounted plasma actuator, when not needed, can be turned off and has low impact on the system. Furthermore, an electronic actuator, unlike a mechanical actuator, has the possibility of matching short time scales inherent in the flow.

The plasma actuator mainly consists of two electrodes with a dielectric sandwiched between them, as shown in Figure 1. Its operation principles have been discussed by Corke, Lon Enloe, and Wilkinson (2010). A simple description is as follows: the plasma is generated between the exposed electrode and the dielectric when high alternating-current (AC) voltage is applied to the exposed electrode. The plasma ions are accelerated in the electric field and collide with air molecules. As a result, flow is induced in the direction from the exposed electrode to the insulated electrode (Font and Morgan 2005).
Figure 1.
Schematic of a DBD plasma actuator.

Many experimental and computational studies have shown the applicability of the plasma actuator for separation control in the low-to-mid Reynolds number flow regime. As examples of two-dimensional airfoil flows, NACA airfoils (Post and Corke 2004, 2006; Bénard, Jolibois, and Moreau 2009; Mabe et al. 2009; Vorobiev, Rennie, and Jumper 2008, 2013), a flat-plate airfoil (Greenblatt et al. 2008; Greenblatt, Schneider, and Schuele 2012), and a low Reynolds number airfoil (Rizzetta and Visbal 2011a, 2011b) have been investigated. Other applications include a linear cascade of turbine blades (Huang, Corke, and Thomas 2006a, 2006b; Van Ness II, Corke, and Morris 2012), a vertical-axis wind turbine (Greenblatt, Ben-Harav, and Mueller-Vahl 2014), and cylinder and bluff-body flows (Jukes and Choi 2009a, 2009b; Li, Zhang, and Huang 2010; Rizzetta and Visbal 2009). All of these studies have shown improvement in aerodynamic performance for each type of fluid machinery through separation control using the plasma actuator. The influence of the actuator configuration (Rizzetta and Visbal 2011b; Riherd and Roy 2013; Visbal, Gaitonde, and Roy 2006; Sekimoto et al. 2012) and the optimum input parameters of the input AC voltage (Enloe et al. 2004; Tsubakino, Tanaka, and Fujii 2007; Sidorenko et al. 2007; Goksel et al. 2006; Patel et al. 2008; Huang, Corke, and Thomas 2006a; Li et al. 2010; Greenblatt et al. 2008; Bénard, Jolibois, and Moreau 2009; Sosa et al. 2011; Greenblatt, Schneider, and Schuele 2012) have also been investigated. In particular, Sato et al. (2013) conducted a massive parametric study and presented a comprehensive discussion about the influence of the parameters of the plasma actuator.

As mentioned above, one of the advantages of the plasma actuator is its high-speed responsiveness, which makes it promising for use in devices that encounter sudden changes in the airstream. This advantage is particularly useful for UAVs and MAVs application. In these, the flow is often laminar because of the relatively low Reynolds number and thus susceptible to separation even with small changes due to momentarily changing situations such as gusts.

When separation occurs due to changing flow conditions, whether because of rapid changes in angle of attack or due to gusts, the transient states by which the uncontrolled state yields the controlled one are important since they establish the time scale over which control authority is established. Although there are many studies on the quasi-steady state of the controlled flow, there have been very few efforts that examine the transient states. In the context of synthetic jet control, Amitay and Glezer (2002) discussed experimental observations of massively separated flow control at the post-stall angle. For the plasma actuators of interest in the current paper, Riherd et al. (2011) investigated the transient processes occurring when controlling moderate separation at the trailing edge at a low angle of attack. They discussed the convergence time to controlled states and independence of the actuator magnitude.

The objective of this study is to investigate the transient processes by which separation is suppressed gradually at the post-stall angle. We use high-fidelity simulations, based on large-eddy simulations using a very high-order compact difference scheme, to focus on the dependence of initial conditions and the frequency effect of the excitation on the physical phenomena observed during the control process.

sec.title: Governing equations
Modelling of the plasma actuator
sec.p:
In Equations (2) and (3), the body force effects are represented as DcSi and DcukSk. Si denotes the non-dimensional body force vector. Many body force models have been proposed for the plasma actuator, including those in Shang and Huang (2014) and Kotsonis et al. (2011), Kriegseis et al. (2013). We use the Suzen model described in Suzen et al. (2005), Suzen and Huang (2006). Figure 2 shows the distribution of the body force in the x direction, where the grey area represents the airfoil region. Although the Suzen model is a relatively simple two-dimensional model compared to other recent models, its reliability has been documented by Nishida, Nonomura, and Abe (2014), who conducted two- and three-dimensional discharge plasma simulations of the plasma actuator. Their results indicate that the spanwise-averaged body force in the three-dimensional simulation has the same characteristics in spatial distribution and time evolution as the results of the two-dimensional simulation. They have also indicated that the induced velocity in a quiescent field by their averaged two-dimensional body force agrees with that by the Suzen model when the net input momentum and the operating conditions of the actuator are the same. This result implies that the sensitivity of the body force model for the induced flow is relatively small, and the Suzen model is reliable as the body force model used in this study.
Figure 2.
Force distribution of the Suzen model.

To choose the appropriate Dc value, we conducted many precomputations on the induced flow field from the plasma actuator in a quiescent field using the distribution in Figure 2. From these results, the Dc values used in this paper were set to ensure that the maximum induced velocity becomes a realistic velocity corresponding to the flow condition of this study. From our experiments, the maximum induced velocity from the steady actuation in a quiescent field was shown to be approximately 1.0 m/s using 6 kV (Vpp) as the AC voltage. This velocity corresponds to the case with Dc ≈ 5 in the present simulation.

sec.title: Implementation of body force
sec.p: Although the detailed mechanisms associated with the charged particle dynamics remain to be clarified (Enloe et al. 2006; Font, Enloe, and McLaughlin 2010; Bérnad, Debien, and Moreau 2013), validations of the body force model, induced flow and controlled flow field, presented in this paper, show that the actuator model used in the present simulation is sufficiently reliable.

sec.title: Computational approach
sec.p: The LANS3D solver (Fujii 1990; Fujii and Obayashi 1989), developed at ISAS/JAXA (Aono et al. 2013), was adopted for the present simulations. The three-dimensional compressible Navier–Stokes equations were solved in generalised curvilinear coordinates (ξ, η, ζ). The spatial derivatives of the convective and viscous terms, metrics, and Jacobian were evaluated by a sixth-order compact difference scheme (Lele 1992). Near the computational boundaries, including inner boundaries resulting from domain decomposition, a second-order one-sided and central formulae at the first and second grid points off the boundaries were used to evaluate the spatial derivatives because of unavailability of a complete stencil of the sixth-order compact difference scheme. To reduce the influence of these boundary treatments, 10 grid points were overlapped at each computational domain boundary. A tenth-order filter (Lele 1992; Gaitonde and Visbal 2000) was applied with a coefficient of 0.495. At the computational domain boundaries, the high-order one-sided formula proposed by Visbal et al. (Visbal and Gaitonde 1999; Gaitonde and Visbal 2000) was employed. A backward second-order difference method with five sub-iterations (Visbal and Rizzetta 2002) was employed for time integration, specifically, the lower–upper symmetric alternating direction implicit and symmetric Gauss–Seidel (Iizuka 2006; Nishida and Nonomura 2009) method. The time increment, which is non-dimensionalised by the free-stream velocity and chord length, was set to 2 × 10−4 in order to achieve a maximum Courant–Friedrichs–Lewy number of less than approximately 2.0. From previous studies on the turbulent boundary layer (Teramoto 2005), this time-step size is confirmed to be sufficient for a large-eddy simulation of wall-bounded turbulence. The high-order, low-pass filter selectively damps only unresolved high-frequency waves, providing closure in an implicit large-eddy simulation approach. Therefore, there are no additional stress and heat flux terms employed for sub-grid closure. At the outflow boundary, all variables were extrapolated from the interior, while the static pressure was fixed to that of the free stream. No-slip and adiabatic conditions were adopted for the wall boundary, and a periodic boundary condition was used in the spanwise direction. Parallel computing was performed using message passing interfaces. All of the computations were conducted by the ‘K’ supercomputer at the Advanced Institute of Computational Science, using approximately 3200 cores (400 nodes).

sec.title: Computational grids
sec.p:
Figure 4 shows an overview and a zoomed-in view of the mesh near the leading edge, using every fifth point. A zonal method was applied to use another fine mesh around the plasma actuator (Fujii 1995). Therefore, there are two grids corresponding to the airfoil grid (zone 1) and the actuator grid (zone 2). A C-type grid was used for zone 1. The computation procedure consists of the following steps. First, the body force with the Suzen model was calculated by an ultrafine grid over the body force region shown in Figure 2. Next, the distribution of the body force obtained in the previous step was mapped to zone 2. In the large-eddy simulation, Equations (1), (2), and (3) in zones 1 and 2 were solved by interpolating the physical values between each zone. The exterior boundary was located at 25 times the chord length from the airfoil surface, and the spanwise region was set to 0.2 times the chord length.
Figure 4.
Computational grids.

A detailed mesh resolution study has been performed using three different meshes, using sizes of 9.8M, 20M, and 46.5M points. The results on controlled and uncontrolled cases, including pressure coefficients, mean, and fluctuating velocities for both the medium and fine meshes agree well with each other, as discussed in Asada (2014). The results in this paper are thus based on a 20M point mesh, distributed among zones 1 and 2 as in Table 1.

In addition, the grid sizes based on the wall unit calculated for attached flows, are (Δξ+, Δη+, Δζ+) ≤ (8, 9, 1). Kawai and Fujii (2008) have suggested that sufficient grid resolutions to resolve near-wall turbulence are Δx+ ≃ 36 in streamwise direction, Δz+ ≃ 15 in spanwise direction and Δy+ ≃ 1 in the wall-normal direction with the same differential and filtering schemes of this study. Therefore, grid sizes used in this study are considered to be sufficient to resolve near-wall turbulence. Also, another zone with fine grid is adopted around the actuator to capture the induced flow by the body force.

sec.title: Flow conditions and cases
sec.p: The conditions and cases chosen are designed to facilitate understanding of transient processes in the separated and controlled flows. The angle of attack is set to 12°, corresponding to post-stall, with a massively separated uncontrolled flow. The Reynolds number is the same as the experiment of Asada et al. (2009), 63,000 based on chord length. In this study, the free-stream velocity and the chord length of the NACA 0015 airfoil is assumed as 1 m/s and 1 m, respectively, and the parameter controlling the relative magnitude of the actuator force, Dc, is set to Dc = 1. Thus, the induced velocity by the actuator force corresponds to approximately 0.3 m/s, which is a realistic value. It should be noted that the present authors also conducted simulations with the airfoil and the plasma actuator at the same conditions as the experimental study of Asada et al. (2009) and validated the present computational methods in a separate study (Sato et al. 2014; Asada et al. 2014). Although the length scale of the modelled actuator is 10 times smaller than in the experimental study, its influence was investigated in a series of studies which confirmed that there is no significant difference on the quasi-steady flow if the Reynolds number and the momentum coefficient of the plasma actuator are almost the same. Two characteristic cases from the previous study of Sato et al. (2013) are chosen. In the present simulations, the free-stream Mach number was set to be 0.2. As shown in Asada (2014), this yields no significant compressibility effects, but does allow for a larger time increment and thus lower costs. The specific heat ratio and the Prandtl number were set to 1.4 and 0.72, respectively.

sec.title: Data processing
sec.p:
In order to extract coherent flow features and examine flow statistics, ensemble averages of 20 computations are conducted for each computational case. Every controlled computation is started from a different time step of the uncontrolled case fields and the controlled transients of flow reattachments are gathered and averaged. The 20 start times are labelled ‘station 01’ to ‘station 20’ and are delayed from each other by one characteristic time (tU∞/c = 1), corresponding to 25,000 steps, as shown in Figure 5. Unsteady flow data are stored at each 10 time steps and every second grid point in each direction for a total of 200,000 time steps (tU∞/c = 8), which is found to be sufficient.
Figure 5.
Histories of lift coefficients CL for select simulations employed for ensemble averages.

sec.title: Unsteady characteristics of aerodynamic coefficients
sec.p:
Figure 6 shows time histories of the lift coefficient CL obtained with the burst actuation F+ = 1 for the different realisations. The time is normalised by c/U∞ and start times of the computations are translated to zero. This allows the burst periods, marked in the figure, to be synchronised for each case. Figure 7 shows time histories of the lift coefficient CL ensemble averages obtained with burst actuation frequencies F+ of 1 and 6. The solid lines denote the ensemble average values of CL and the filled areas denote the range, i.e., the upper lines denote maximum CL values of all stations, and the lower lines denote minimum CL values of all stations.
Figure 6.
Time histories of the lift coefficient CL obtained with the burst actuation F+ = 1. The time is normalised by c/U∞. ‘ON’ denotes the duration in which the DBD plasma actuator is actuated, and ‘OFF’ denotes the duration in which the DBD plasma actuator is not actuated.
Figure 7.
Time histories of the lift coefficient CL obtained with the burst actuation F+ = 1, 6. The time is normalised by c/U∞. The solid line denotes the ensemble-average values of CL and the colour-filled areas denote the possible value areas.

Several observations can be made about the unsteady characteristics. First, each CL curve converges on a quasi-steady value which is almost the same as the ensemble-averaged value, although initial CL values are quite-variable among stations. Second, the transient times in the two cases are of the same order and in the range of approximately 4 to 6 and the CL of the F+ = 6 case converges relatively quickly. Third, for both cases, large lift decreases are observed in the initial transients (tU∞/c ∼ 1.5). This large lift decrease is caused by advection of a spanwise vortex which entrains the free stream. Further discussion is presented in Section 5.3 in the context of ensemble averages.

Figure 8 shows time histories of the drag coefficient CD obtained with the burst actuation F+ = 1, 6, obtained in the same manner as in Figure 7. The solid lines denote the ensemble average values of CD and the colour-filled areas denote the ranges. The same trends are observed with CD as with CL, including the lack of dependence on initial conditions, similar transient times in the two cases, and initial decreases in CD for the same reasons, i.e., entrainment increases suction side pressure and thus reduces the drag.
Figure 8.
Time histories of the drag coefficient CD obtained with the burst actuation F+ = 1, 6. The time is normalised by c/U∞. The solid line denotes the ensemble-average values of CD and the colour-filled areas denote the possible value areas.

The transients can thus be categorised into following three stages (Figure 9): (1) the lift and drag decreasing stage,(2) the lift recovering stage, and(3) the lift and drag converging stage. The details of each stage are discussed in the following sections.
Figure 9.
Schematic of the characteristic transient stages.

sec.title: Instantaneous flow fields
sec.p:
The instantaneous fields provide insight into the three stages identified above. Figures 10 and 11 show instantaneous flow fields obtained with the burst actuation F+ = 1, 6. The iso-surfaces are the second invariant of the velocity gradient tensors (Q-criterion) coloured by chord-directional velocity. In the F+ = 1 case, the effect of control is to enhance free-stream entrainment as observed near mid-chord of Figure 10(a). This is the result of the advection of the spanwise vortex, which is generated by the first actuation of the DBD plasma actuator. Similar flow is found in Figure 11(a). This spanwise vortex can be clearly found in the ensemble-averaged flow fields which are discussed in the next section. After the first actuation, one or two spanwise vortices are generated upstream (x/c ∼ 0.3) and merge into one large vortex downstream (x/c ∼ 0.6) every burst period. With the passage of the burst period, the inclination of the separated shear layer is reduced, and the accelerated flow region near the leading edge (0 $\lesssim $ x/c $\lesssim $ 0.2) gradually increases in size. On the other hand, for the F+ = 6 case, the separated region (u/U∞ ≤ 0) near the trailing edge becomes smaller more rapidly than the F+ = 1 case (Figure 11(b)). Several strong spanwise vortices are generated, which subsequently break down to finer three-dimensional vortices near the middle of the airfoil surface (tU∞/c = 3 − 4). The three-dimensional vortices are then induced again by vortex merging of the stronger spanwise vortices. At tU∞/c = 8, the flow is quasi-steady and the three-dimensional vortices are more prevalent.
Figure 10.
Instantaneous flow fields obtained with the burst actuation F+ = 1. Colour contour is a chord-directional velocity and iso-surfaces are second invariant of the velocity gradient tensors Q-criterion.
Figure 11.
Instantaneous flow fields obtained with the burst actuation F+ = 6. Colour contour is a chord-directional velocity and iso-surfaces are second invariant of the velocity gradient tensors Q-criterion.

sec.title: Ensemble-averaged flow fields
sec.p:
Figures 12 and 13 show ensemble-averaged flow fields obtained with the two burst actuation frequencies at tU∞/c = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8. The contour surface is a chord-directional velocity and contour lines are of the Q-criterion. The large spanwise vortex evident at x/c ∼ 0.8 in every frame of Figure 12 is generated by actuation of every burst periods. The high-speed region observed at the mid-chord near the airfoil surface is the result of advection of the spanwise vortex which entrains the free stream to the airfoil surface. As noted earlier, this effect increases suction side pressure and reduces CL. This CL decrease is also observed in the initial stage of transient state (tU∞/c ∼ 1.5) in Figure 7. After the first actuation, several spanwise vortices are generated downstream of the actuators (x/c ∼ 0.3). These merge into one larger vortex downstream (x/c ∼ 0.6) every burst period.
Figure 12.
Ensemble-averaged flow fields obtained with the burst actuation F+ = 1. Colour contour is a chord-directional velocity and black contour lines are second invariant of the velocity gradient tensors Q-criterion.
Figure 13.
Ensemble-averaged flow fields obtained with the burst actuation F+ = 6. Colour contour is a chord-directional velocity and black contour lines are second invariant of the velocity gradient tensors Q-criterion.

Some of the observations carry over to the F+ = 6 case (Figure 13). For example, a high-speed region is observed at the middle of chord length near the airfoil surface. However, the separation region near the leading edge is relatively smaller than the flow of F+ = 1. Likewise, the separated region near the trailing edge is also smaller (Figure 13(b)), but at tU∞/c ∼ 5.0, it cycles from large to small. This sequence of trailing separation relates to advection of the vortices generated by the DBD plasma actuator. First, several spanwise strong vortices are generated, e.g., at least eight vortices are observed at tU∞/c ∼ 4.0. These vortices then reduce to six at tU∞/c ∼ 8.0, corresponding to the non-dimensional burst frequency. Subsequently, this vortex merging induces fine three-dimensional vortices which weaken the spanwise vortices. The accelerated flow region near the leading edge becomes large gradually as for the F+ = 1 case.

Figures 14 and 15 show pressure coefficients Cp obtained from the ensemble-averaged flow with the burst actuation F+ = 1 and F+ = 6 along the airfoil. At tU∞/c ∼ 1.0, a high-pressure region is observed on the suction side mid-chord, consistent with the previously mentioned vortex dynamics. Near the leading edge, the plateau distribution of Cp, which is caused by the separation bubble, is found at every time stage. With the passage of the burst period, the peak negative pressure tracks the gradual development of accelerated flow region near the leading edge.
Figure 14.
Ensemble-averaged pressure coefficients Cp obtained with the burst actuation F+ = 1 along the airfoil.
Figure 15.
Ensemble-averaged pressure coefficients Cp obtained with the burst actuation F+ = 6 along the airfoil.

In the F+ = 6 case, a high-pressure region is also found at the mid-chord on the suction side, at tU∞/c ∼ 1.0. Local Cp oscillations in the range tU∞/c ∼ 2.0 to tU∞/c ∼ 5.0, are enhanced by the spanwise vortices, but gradually disappear because of vortex merging. This process is accompanied by the induction of finer three-dimensional vortices which diffuse the energy of spanwise vortices, increasing the fullness of the velocity profile, thus reducing local Cp oscillations.

Figures 16 and 17 show the skin-friction coefficients Cf obtained from the ensemble-averaged flows with burst actuation F+ = 1 and F+ = 6. In these figures, positive and negative regions denote attached and separated regions. The attached region at mid-chord at tU∞/c ∼ 1.0, corresponds to the high-pressure region in the Figure 14. The initiation of attachment is associated with entrainment of the free stream towards the airfoil. Again, there are many qualitative similarities between the F+ = 1 and F+ = 6 cases, including the mid-chord attached region, strong spanwise vortex growth and merging to result in an almost attached flow by x/c = 0.2.
Figure 16.
Ensemble-averaged skin-friction coefficients Cf obtained with the burst actuation F+ = 1 on the suction side of the airfoil.
Figure 17.
Ensemble-averaged skin-friction coefficients Cf obtained with the burst actuation F+ = 6 on the suction side of the airfoil.

Finally, the stages by which the actuator induces attachment are discussed by analysing the Reynolds shear stresses. Figures 18 and 19 show Reynolds shear stresses ($-u^{\prime }v^{\prime }/U_{\infty }^2$) obtained from the ensemble-averaged flow fields for F+ = 1 and F+ = 6, respectively.
Figure 18.
Ensemble-averaged flow fields obtained with the burst actuation F+ = 1. Colour contour is a Reynolds shear stress ($\langle -u^{\prime }v^{\prime }\rangle /U_{\infty }^2$) and black contour lines are second invariant of the velocity gradient tensors Q-criterion.
Figure 19.
Ensemble-averaged flow fields obtained with the burst actuation F+ = 6. Colour contour is a Reynolds shear stress ($\langle -u^{\prime }v^{\prime }\rangle /U_{\infty }^2$) and black contour lines are second invariant of the velocity gradient tensors Q-criterion.

The results can be connected to the basic characteristics of the flow fields discussed earlier in Figures 12 and 13. The large spanwise vortex generated by the first actuation, observed at x/c ∼ 0.8 in Figure 18(a), is accompanied by strong growth of the Reynolds shear stress. At tU∞/c = 2, the strong Reynolds-shear-stress area is found near the large spanwise vortex. Although this correlation between the vortex and Reynolds stresses continues even after tU∞/c = 3, the magnitude of the stress is diminished. On the other hand, the magnitude of the stress near the reattachment point, x/c ∼ 0.25, gradually becomes stronger.

In the F+ = 6 case, a strong Reynolds-shear-stress area is also found around the large spanwise vortex at tU∞/c = 1. This area disappears relatively earlier as compared to F+ = 1 case, and another strong Reynolds-shear-stress region appears near the trailing edge (see tU∞/c = 4 frame). This high stress is caused by vortex merging of strong spanwise vortices, as mentioned in the previous section. The enhanced Reynolds-shear-stress region propagates upstream and gradually concentrates near the reattachment point (x/c ∼ 0.2) at the quasi-steady state, being maintained by fine three-dimensional vortices which enhance mixing of the flow and keep the flow attached. These results indicate that spanwise vortices play an important role in suppressing the flow separation at the initial stage of the transient state, while the three-dimensional vortices play an important role closer to the quasi-steady state.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: The transient processes by which a plasma actuator exerts control authority are discussed by considering an ACDBD actuator located at 5% chord length and operating at reduced burst frequencies of F+ = 1 and F+ = 6. The results are discussed primarily through ensemble-averaged statistical analyses of 20 computations using different initial conditions. Although initial CL and CD values vary significantly for each run, they converge to the same quasi-steady values, demonstrating that the initial flow conditions do not affect the quasi-steady state if the separation is suppressed. The transient times on the two cases are of the same order and in the range approximately four to six characteristic times based on free-stream velocity and chord length. The transient states can be categorised into three stages corresponding to an initial temporary lift and drag reduction stage, a lift recovery stage, and a lift and drag converging stage. The first stage is characterised by the introduction of a spanwise vortex through the first actuation, followed by entrainment. At the second stage, the separated shear layer near the leading edge gradually approaches the airfoil surface, and the accelerated flow region near the leading edge gradually becomes large. This widening of the accelerated flow region contributes to the rapid increase of CL. In this stage, the spanwise vortices are dominant. At the third stage, flow slowly approaches the quasi-steady state in which the spanwise vortices are weakened by the fine three-dimensional vortices. These dissipation phenomena contribute to the reduction of the local flow-separation. Thus, at the initial stage of the transient state, spanwise vortices play an important role in suppressing the flow separation. On the other hand, the three-dimensional vortices play the corresponding role at the quasi-steady state.
